#813. Raphinha sees red as Brazil stunned by Japan while Argentina’s post-Messi era starts with defeat

Brazil loss in Singapore marred by unruly end to friendly

Argentina beaten 2-1 by Uruguay in Buenos Aires

Raphinha was sent off as Brazil crashed to a 3-2 defeat by Japan in their international friendly in Singapore. The Barcelona captain had been substituted after 71 minutes, but was shown a red card after protesting against Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s stoppage-time winner on the touchline. The Brazil head coach, Carlo Ancelotti, was also sent off in a fractious ending to the match.

Japan went 2-0 up inside 20 minutes through Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura. Vinícius Júnior reduced the deficit in the 33rd minute and scored again to drag them level on 75 minutes, before Sakamoto’s controversial late winner.

Argentina’s post-Messi era began with a 2-1 defeat at home against Uruguay in Buenos Aires. The loss marked the World Cup finalists’ first match since Lionel Messi’s international retirement in early October.

Leonardo Balerdi opened the scoring with an own goal in the 48th minute, before Maximiliano Araújo doubled Uruguay’s lead in the 53rd minute under their new coach, Diego Forlán. Julián Álvarez pulled one back for the hosts in the 73rd minute.

This clásico rioplatense on Friday also kicked off a new chapter for Argentina under Lionel Scaloni, who extended his contract to 2030 this week.

Messi’s retirement remains a fresh wound for local fans; notably, the La Bombonera stadium fell short of a sellout, a rare departure from the norm. While most supporters in the stands wore the albiceleste jersey with Messi’s No 10, Scaloni chose not to assign the number for the match. The coach explained he has yet to select a successor and as it is not mandatory he prefers to leave the jersey vacant for now.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

On the pitch, Argentina lacked the explosive, incisive spark Messi typically produced in the final third. Neither Nicolás Paz nor Thiago Almada was able to fill that void. Argentina will hope to bounce back against Costa Rica in Córdoba on Tuesday, while Uruguay host the Dominican Republic on the same day.

#811. Pakistani astronaut set to become 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station this month

"Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An astronaut from Pakistan is set to launch on China's Shenzhou 24 mission in the coming weeks and become the first-ever international visitor to the Tiangong space station.

A pair of astronaut candidates from Pakistan have been training at the Astronaut Centre of China in Beijing, following an agreement reached between China and Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025 and a subsequent selection process.

China's human spaceflight agency confirmed in a Nov. 7 press statement that the upcoming Shenzhou 24 mission will carry one of the astronauts. The agency also released a mission patch.

"China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Nov. 9. "Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program."

It is not yet known which of the two candidates will fly on Shenzhou 24. They were named in Pakistani press reports as Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, both pilots from the country's military forces. The pair were chosen from a wider pool of around 20 finalists.

The chosen candidate will fly as a payload specialist on Shenzhou 24 along with two Chinese colleagues, while the other will be on standby as a backup. While the Chinese astronauts will be starting a six-month-long stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will spend roughly a week in orbit aboard Tiangong during a standard crew rotation period. He will then return to Earth aboard the departing Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, along with two Chinese astronauts who will have completed a six-month-long stay in orbit.

The arrangement means changes to China's usual "three in, three out" Tiangong crew rotations. One of the three Shenzhou 23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong on May 24, will stay aboard and complete China's first-ever year-long stay in orbit, while the Pakistani astronaut will take their seat aboard Shenzhou 23 to return home.

During his stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will be responsible for four research payloads selected from more than 300 proposals, according to Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO.

China has not announced a timeline for the launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission, but it is expected to lift off before the end of November. The Shenzhou 23 astronauts currently aboard Tiangong are closing in on 180 days in orbit, nearing an end to their six months in space.

Shenzhou 24 will launch from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert on a Long March 2F rocket. The identities of the crew for China's human spaceflight missions are typically closely guarded, and will only be revealed in a press conference a day ahead of launch. Shenzhou 24's Long March 2F rocket will be rolled out to the pad around a week ahead of launch.

The partnership between the two countries has already produced Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites, including a lunar cubesat, and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on the Chang'e-8 lunar landing mission.

Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

#809. Portugal immortalise Cristiano Ronaldo’s No 7 shirt in tribute to national legend

Original No 7 design preserved to honour player

Career brought 146 goals and three major titles

Portugal have made a permanent change to the No 7 shirt to honour the legacy of Cristiano Ronaldo and ensure the number remains forever associated with their greatest footballing icon.

The former forward, whose career spanned 23 years and 246 caps in which he scored 146 goals, announced his retirement on 5 November after a falling out with coach Jorge Jesus. His last appearance for Portugal was on 24 September, in a 1-0 home win over Wales in the Nations League.

Before their Nations League clash against Denmark, Portugal tweeted a unique design change to the iconic No 7 shirt to ensure Ronaldo’s version remains immortalised.

The small change to the number 7 is an acknowledgement of the star’s playing career in which he broke the men’s all-time scoring record. He captained his country to their first major trophy at Euro 2016, before adding two Nations League titles in 2019 and 2025.

Portugal will also pay tribute to Ronaldo before and during their Nations League fixture against Denmark in Braga on Saturday.

“Time to debut a new 7. Because there’s one that will be eternal,” the Portuguese national team wrote on social media on Saturday. The post included a goat emoji to signify “Greatest Of All Time”.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It also included a video that showed a horizontal crossed line through the No 7 as it is commonly written in Europe, suggesting that Ronaldo’s successors will all have that cross to bear when they wear the number.

#808. Chelsea go top of WSL as Sandy Baltimore bullet sees off Manchester City

Pragmatic, resolute and gutsy. Sonia Bompastor showed her ruthless side and delivered a tactical masterclass as Chelsea earned a 1-0 win over Manchester City and leapfrogged them at the top of the Women’s Super League.

Lucy Bronze credited fellow full-back Katie McCabe with firing Chelsea up pre-match, having told them they “had to be dogs” in the game, and a dogged performance followed. Sandy Baltimore’s stunning strike in added time at the end of the first half was the difference as the west London side nullified the threat of a team that had scored in each of their preceding 21 games in all competitions, inflicting their first loss of the campaign.

The task for City got even tougher when goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita received a straight red for clattering into Alyssa Thompson, but despite their numerical disadvantage it was end to end right up until the final whistle.

“It always affects you when you go one player down,” said manager Andrée Jeglertz. “But we handled that and that’s not why we lose the game. I think it’s small details. It’s a tight game, it’s two great football teams, there’s a lot of situations, there’s a lot of battles and they managed to score on their big chance from a great finish. We also have a couple of great opportunities where we don’t manage to score.”

Momentum was with City going into the match after their 5-0 defeat of West Ham the preceding weekend and a 4-1 win against Inter in the Champions League on Tuesday night and they were able to welcome the injured duo Vivianne Miedema and Beth Mead back to the bench to bolster their matchday squad.

At Stamford Bridge the England women’s manager, Sarina Wiegman, the US women’s manager, Emma Hayes, and passionate women’s football advocate and pundit Ian Wright were in the stands. It was a fixture that promised much, and it delivered: the league’s most potent attacks, with Chelsea having scored 28 league goals before this fixture to City’s 27, while Bompastor’s side had the most solid defence, having conceded only five times before kick-off.

Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier marked her 150th appearance for the club with a superb strike in a 2-0 victory over Crystal Palace at the Progress with Unity Stadium. Presented with a framed shirt before kick-off, Le Tissier whipped a low shot from distance into the net in the 18th minute before Elisabeth Terland confirmed United’s win after the hour mark.

United moved up to fourth with the win and they kept hold of the position after Tottenham drew a blank in a goalless draw at home to Everton, whose winless run in the league stretched to five matches. In the day’s late game, Liverpool ended a five-match winless run in the WSL by easing past Brighton 3-0. Press Association

It was a chess match. After a thrillingly frenetic start there was a change for Chelsea just 12 minutes in, with the centre-back Kadeisha Buchanan replaced by Veerle Buurman. There was speculation over whether the withdrawal of the Canadian defender was due to injury and Bompastor unconvincingly claimed it was.

“Yesterday in training, she got a knock to her head during contact with a teammate. She was fine after the training session. She was fine in the evening. We assessed her again this morning and everything was fine,” she said. “I just felt watching her from the beginning of the game, she was not herself. Then I took the responsibility to make the substitution. But for me, I was almost forced to do that because I know my player and I know she was not in the game.”

However, if, as many believe, the defensive switch was a tactical decision, it was a stroke of genius, as Buurman was excellent at nullifying the threat of Khadija Shaw.

“She had a really good performance against a top player,” said Bompastor. “Today was positive. But again, as I’ve told you previously, when it doesn’t work it’s not so positive.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

There were chances at both ends but they were limited and it took until the fourth of five added minutes for Chelsea to draw first blood. The goal was sensational. Baltimore collected the ball just inside the box on the right, from Ellie Carpenter, lined up her shot and sent a piledriver of a strike into the roof of the net.

It was the only shot on target in the first half.

City sought an instant reply after the break but they could not find a way through and momentum ebbed and flowed. Jeglertz withdrew Sam Coffey and Mary Fowler in favour of Miedema and Laura Blindkilde Brown to help his side assert some authority in the middle and, through Miedema, to add some creative instinct.

However, as City pushed they left themselves vulnerable on the break and when Maika Hamano’s crossfield ball was met by Alyssa Thompson with just over 15 minutes remaining it was disaster for City. Yamashita raced out of her box and clattered into the Chelsea forward, conceding a free-kick and receiving a straight red card.

Despite City’s efforts, Chelsea were in control and they held strong to blow the title race wide open.

#807. Clough's longevity: landmark achievement or indictment on football?

Nigel Clough took charge of Mansfield Town in November 2020

Becoming the longest-serving manager at a club takes some doing in the fickle world of football.

Sticking around at two clubs long enough to hold that mantle is just about unprecedented.

But Mansfield Town's Nigel Clough is about to redefine longevity as a manager when it comes to working at sides that make up the top 92 in the English pyramid.

"I don't think it's particularly an achievement; I think it's more an indictment of football that nobody else has lasted that long," Clough told BBC Sport.

This weekend he becomes the longest-serving manager â in terms of active years in the job and league matches at the helm â of the Stags, where he surpasses club great Ian Greaves.

The 16 years Clough spent at Burton Albion, which took in around 900 matches across two spells spanning more than two decades, means the record at the east Staffordshire side is already his.

Former England forward Clough is now six years and one week into the Stags job and is the second longest-serving manager across England's top four leagues - behind only Mikel Arteta at Arsenal - but he does not see his staying power as anything special.

"I don't really think about it that much, I have to say. I'm just trying to get through the week," said Clough, who has been in charge of Mansfield for 329 matches across all competitions.

While Clough's players, as well as Mansfield fans have a different take on what his lengthy tenure at the One Call Stadium has meant, the 60-year-old reeled off the names of legendary past managers - his late father and iconic Nottingham Forest boss Brian Clough included - when reflecting on what joy clubs would have by sticking by their manager.

"When you look back 20 or 30 years, my dad was at Forest for 18 years, Alex Ferguson was at Manchester United for so long and then there was Arsene Wenger at Arsenal. That was at the top level, but even lower down there was a lot of managers who stayed a lot of years," he said

"I just think it's sad the way football is going at the moment. The first bad period that people have, a month, two months or something like that, and the manager is the one that goes."

Clough, who played in the top flight for Forest, Liverpool and Manchester City, has been in management for 28 years and been in charge of just four clubs - Mansfield, Burton, Derby County and Sheffield United - in that time.

Since bounding from non-league level - where he spent the first 10 years of his management career in his first spell at Burton - to take the reins of Derby in the Championship in 2009, no-one has overseen more matches than Clough's 893 across England's top four divisions.

The latest statistics from the League Managers' Association show that managers across those leagues are now staying in their jobs for less than a year on average.

Clough bucking the trend with his record-setting endurance at Mansfield comes in the same week that Manchester United sacked Michael Carrick, when he was 10 months into the job, and Crystal Palace relieved Pierre Sage of his role after only 16 games.

When asked if Clough has ever felt his job was under threat during any "sticky period" at Mansfield, he responded with a firm "of course".

It was when the Stags were in the relegation places and on a 12-match winless run in his first full campaign in charge in 2021-22.

He survived that, then oversaw a club-record 11 consecutive home wins and went on to guide Mansfield to the League Two play-off final at Wembley later the same season.

"You've got to go through that period and you've got to get through it," Clough said of dealing with difficult runs as a manager.

"And I think as you get a little bit older, you know more that it's going to change.

"You get a result out of adversity as much as anything. If you're winning, it doesn't keep going, and if you're losing it's the same thing if you've got a reasonable team and you're doing the right things."

Clough: 'Six years have gone extremely quickly'

Mansfield boss Clough on 25 years 'in family business'

Nigel Clough's Mansfield side are 11th in the League One table after 13 games this season

While Mansfield missed out on promotion when they took their bid all the way to the national stadium in 2022, they went up automatically two years later when they finished third in the table.

It ended Mansfield's 21-year absence from the third tier. And when he kept them up in their first season back, Clough did what no-one had done for 35 years.

Last season they finished 10th, the club's highest league placing since 1987 when Greaves guided them to exactly the same position in the standings.

Stags supporter Dean Foulkes says it "has been an incredible journey" at Mansfield since Clough took the helm in November 2020.

At Burton he is a club legend for the way he transformed the Brewers as a non-league side in his first spell there before taking them to the Championship during his second stint.

He leapt a number of divisions when he left Burton the first time to manage Derby - a particularly poignant job as his father took the Rams to their first English title in 1972.

Even at Sheffield United, where Clough had the shortest stint of his managerial career, he guided them to the semi-final of the FA Cup when they were a League One side in 2014.

"He is really good football man to have around. We should be proud that he is Mansfield Town manager," Foulkes told BBC Radio Nottingham.

"Look at what he has achieved, promotion, and we now have players coming to Mansfield Town because they want to play for Nigel Clough."

It is why prolific veteran forward David McGoldrick moved there in the summer, and how the club has enticed former Leeds United forward Tyler Roberts, as well as ex-Preston forward Michael Smith to the Nottinghamshire town while also landing highly-rated Tottenham midfielder George Abbott on loan.

Ryan Sweeney says the chance to play for Clough was "the main reason" he decided to return to the club last summer.

Former Nottingham Forest and Southend striker Stephen McLaughlin says Clough "manages differently to any other manager" he has worked with.

"He doesn't treat you as a number, he treats you as a person and you want to run though bricks walls for him," McLaughlin said.

"It's hard to explain what he does for you on and off the pitch as well. You are not on the grass too long in training because he trusts you to get your work in and to be ready for Saturday.

"He doesn't give too much tactical information to people because the message is 'just do your job and work hard'."

Jordan Bowery has been asked to do that more than most, having been transformed from a striker to a defender and is now seen as 'Mr Versatile'., external

"He is incredibly loyal and trusts me in those positions," Bowery said. "A lot of managers wouldn't do that, but he's had my back and I appreciate that.

"He can get onto you, but that is like most managers. He expects and demands the best out of every single one of you each day.

"He has obviously been around the game a long time, played at the highest level - he knows the game and he knows the players."

A young Nigel Clough (right) pictured in 1978, sat alongside his father Brian in the Nottingham Forest dugout

And Clough, the player, is a former attacker of considerable repute in Nottinghamshire.

No-one has scored more than Clough's 131 goals for Forest over the past 113 years.

It was there, at Mansfield's high-profile county neighbours, where he thrived under his father who famously guided the Reds to the First Division title in 1978 before collecting back-to-back European Cups.

The manager that Clough is has been shaped by the successes he watched up close as a child and those he later revelled in as a player.

"When you're brought up in the household that we were brought up in and the environment we were brought up in, then we have a certain insight into what it takes to have a chance of being successful and what you expect of the team and everything," he said.

"And the empathy, I don't think you should ever forget that if you've been a player as well, how that feels when you have a rough time and so on."

And it is those players, and how they are found before investing in them that is the closest thing to revealing the secret to Clough's longevity.

"We don't like wasting the owners' money," he said.

"Whether it was at Burton when we were in the Dr Martens South [non-league level] or whether it's here at Mansfield Town, we try and look after it as best we can. And we have a responsibility to do that.

"We do as much in-depth research as we can on players. Character is the main feature of what we look at. We can see all the stuff on the videos of what they can do, then we watch them live and everything, but you have to delve really into the character and get a lot of references from players, coaches, managers.

"We take that very seriously. Each season we set out to just try and get a few better players in the squad.

"It's keeping the ball rolling, keeping the owners happy, keeping the supporters happy."

Additional reporting by BBC Radio Nottingham's David Jackson and Jake Garner.

#806. The Rainmaker Kills Off Character With Gruesome Beheading

The Rainmaker season two just killed off a major character, their head found in Bruiser’s designer handbag. Here are all the gory details.

This Rainmaker death will make fans lose their heads.

And in this case, that expression takes on a fairly literal meaning. While it seemed like Tom Cassady (Austin Nichols) had his death sentence written at the close of episode four, he wasn’t the victim of the Nov. 13 episode.

Instead, it was Miss Doppler Dumbass herself. Lynette, Tom’s new wife played by Sarah O’Connor, found her head separated from her body and stuffed into the designer handbag now in the possession of Bruiser (Lana Parrilla).

The beginnings of Lynette’s dark fate were teased in episode four, when it was revealed that Tom’s gambling debts hadn’t actually gotten him—as well as the attorneys of J. Lyman Stone—mixed up with the likes of Gator Jack Guidry (Owen Roe).

Instead, the former pro baseball player was covering for his wife’s own money loss. After all, the weatherwoman was looking for other lucrative avenues when Tom’s pro career (and the buckets of money she thought would come with it) was cut short.

Once Bruiser made the connection, however, she stressed that Lynette and Tom must remain married to ensure they don’t have to test against one another.

So, a drunk Lynette—devastated that she is further chained to her disappointing marriage—rushed to the headquarters of Gator’s operations, begging the crime boss to help her out of her situation.

But while it seemed like he’d take out Tom, Gator felt Lynette to be the looser of the two ends and cut her life short. As for exactly how, where, when and who? That’s all still left to be determined.

For Austin, making the bloody discovery was intimidating.

“There's a funny story behind this,” the actor, who joined season two of the hit show, told USA Network. “We have so many light, fun scenes. And then I remember getting a call sheet and it saying, ‘Tomorrow, you're going to discover your wife's head in a purse.’ And I was like, ‘Oh, okay, I got to act. I got to be serious. I got to do some real work here.’”

As he put it, finding a head in a handbag is “not something you see every day. It's super high stakes.”

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the Euclid space telescope released its first major batch of data, capturing the light of more than a billion objects over an area of sky as big as 9,500 full moons. The data release lays the foundation for one of the largest-ever 3D maps of the cosmos and many groundbreaking discoveries about the nature of dark energy and dark matter.

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has been called the "Dark Universe Detective" because of its capability to investigate the dual mysteries of dark matter, the universe's most mysterious stuff, and dark energy, the force accelerating the expansion of the universe. Collectively, these cosmic elements are sometimes referred to as the dark universe.

The new data release, designated DR1-Foundation, was built from 13 months of observations and is accompanied by a multitude of images, including large sky mosaics. It marks the first major release of mission data since Euclid launched in mid-2023.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," ESA's Director of Science, Carole Mundell said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery in a new regime for astronomy and demonstrating the excellence of European technology, science and international collaboration."

The ESA put into raw numbers the sheer number of celestial objects viewed by the Dark Universe Detective and contained in DR1-Foundation. That includes light spectra from 160 million sources, over 900 million galaxies, and 60 million candidates for quasars, regions of space dominated by feeding supermassive black holes.

"This is a change in scale from Euclid's previous releases, which included a few days of observations over around 60 degrees squared of sky," ESA's Euclid project scientist Valeria Pettorino said. "We're now releasing more than a year of data covering a significantly larger area. This unlocks groundbreaking science."

Euclid can see such a vast number of cosmic objects thanks to the fact that its space-based position helps it avoid interference caused by Earth's atmosphere.

This includes clusters of galaxies and even larger superclusters. The study of these objects, some of the largest structures in the cosmos, can reveal how matter came together across the larger network of gas, dust and dark matter called the cosmic web.

"Euclid doesn't just look far back in time  — it does so across huge areas of sky," Euclid Consortium member Barbara Sartoris of JL Lagrange Laboratory, Nice, France, explained. "This gives us an unprecedented view of large samples of ancient galaxy clusters that were previously out of reach. "We will explore these in the coming months to learn how these giants grew, and decipher what they reveal about the dark universe."

Another exciting element of the new Euclid data release is the 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates catalogued by the space telescope. Gravitational lensing is an element of the universe first explained in Einstein magnum opus, general relativity, in 1915.

General relativity says that objects with mass cause the very fabric of space to warp, and that gravity arises from this warping. But there is another consequence. When light passes this curvature, its usually straight path is curved. That means when light from a single background source passes an object with great mass, like a galaxy or galaxy cluster, a strong gravitational lens, it can arrive at our telescopes at different times.

As a result of this strong lensing, background sources can be greatly amplified. It is an effect that the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has been using to great effect to study galaxies in the early universe.

Thus, the prospect of mapping 15,000 strong gravitational lenses is monumental, especially in studying the rate at which the universe is expanding and thus the effect of dark energy.

"Strong lensing provides unique insight into the dark universe, allowing us to 'weigh' individual galaxies, including their invisible dark matter, and explore how the universe is expanding," Natalie Lines of the University of Portsmouth, U.K., and member of the Euclid Consortium, said. "Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionize the field of strong lens discovery. That day is finally here."

Arguably, the most exciting thing about DR1-Foundation is that Euclid is just getting started. The area of sky covered from spring 2024 to spring 2025 represents just 14% of Euclid's target for its entire six-year survey.

That means whatever scientists discover from this data release could be the tip of the iceberg in terms of how the Dark Universe Detective will change our understanding of the cosmos.

"DR1-Foundation includes raw data, calibrated images, catalogues, and spectra over a huge sky area, with enough statistics touncover even rare objects," Valeria said. "It will be used to map the large-scale structure of the universe in unprecedented detail.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #804. De la Fuente adamant there is no racism in Spain despite England reminder to players

England’s first game in Madrid since racist abuse in 2004

De la Fuente tells Tuchel ‘we’re not racists, none of us’

Luis de la Fuente has told Thomas Tuchel there is no racism in Spain after the England coach’s admission that he would remind his players of the anti-racism protocol prior to their meeting at the Metropolitano on Sunday night.

This will be the first time the countries play each other in Madrid since some of England’s black players were subjected to racist abuse in a match at the Santiago Bernabéu in 2004. And although England have returned to Spain three times without incident since then, twice in Seville and once in Alicante, Tuchel was asked on Friday about going back in the buildup to Sunday’s game. The England coach replied that England “will not expect anything [untoward]” but also said: “maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid].”

Asked to respond to those words, and whether Spain still had work to do combating racism after being fined for discriminatory chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt in Barcelona in March, the Spain coach asked for confirmation as to whom they had come from, then said: “I can say the opposite. Tell Thomas there is no racism. As clear as that. Exactly the same as in England. We’re not racists, none of us.”

Tuchel, speaking later on Saturday night, expressed his irritation with the media, accusing journalists of manufacturing a row. “I got asked ‘what will happen if and if and if’, and I said if it happens, we have a protocol in place. That’s it … I never talked about racism in Spain, I answered politely a question about what happens. You create a lot of confusion for absolutely nothing.”

De la Fuente also described Spain versus England as “one of the best games you can see anywhere in the world right now, maybe the best”, and admitted that his team needs to exercise more control than they had been able to do during their 3-2 win at Wembley in September.

Asked to explain how the Premier League could be the richest league in the world and English players command bigger transfer fees than Spaniards despite the national team not winning anything since 1966 while the selección have won two World Cups and three Euros in this century alone, he insisted that it is a mistake to mix price and value.

“There is a song about value and price and it is exactly that,” the Spain coach said. “Someone has to pay it and that’s very welcome but it doesn’t mean it is the real value. I am surprised often when you see the prices paid for our players compared to [the fees] paid in England. I think ‘they’re so cheap’. They [Spanish players] are the best in the world. You can buy a player for half the price of what you pay in England for someone. In that world, in that market, that’s what’s spent. But I’m clear on this: we must not confuse price and value.”

“Between the English model and the Spanish model, I would choose the Spanish model,” De la Fuente added. “It is recognisable and the players have the ability to express it. The English model has developed a lot and I think it is very good. But you have to have the players. We can’t play like them and they can’t play like us.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“One of the strengths England have is the ability to run into space. When the game is open, they have people who are comfortable with that space and playing that style. Last time against them we lacked control, were unable to have longer periods of possession and impose ourselves more on our opponents.

“In the last two tournaments, England have been third and finalists. I think they are a great team and they have great players. That shows you it is not easy to win. Maybe that should make us appreciate what we’re doing this century: it is marvellous and very difficult. England are always candidates to win everything [nowadays]. This is one of the best games you can see in the world.”

#801. Shane Gillis Breaks Silence on Backlash After Divisive SNL Monologue

Shane Gillis addressed the public response to his controversial Saturday Night Live monologue given during the show's Oct. 10 episode: “’I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad.’”

After the comedian sparked controversy following his monologue as host of Saturday Night Live—where he accused women of dressing like "wh--es" while going to the gym—Gillis is addressing the public fallout, clarifying that producers of the sketch comedy show didn't know of his exact material.

“Not to defend SNL, they don’t approve it. I mean, they could shut it down,” Gillis, 38, said during his appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience Nov. 13. “They could, but you don’t write your set and give it to them. Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics; they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them.”

The Bupkis actor noted he did share his own expectations of the Oct. 10 episode.

“The funniest part was, they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’” he explained. “And I was like, ‘It’s not great but I don’t say anything bad.’ The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for f--king 10 minutes. That’s it.'”

As for addressing his commentary about women’s gym attire, Gillis noted, “For the record, don’t have a problem with it. It’s wonderful.”

ICYMI, during his monologue—which elicited critiques from celebs including Dan Levy, Inde Navarrette and more, as well as stars coming to his defense such as David Spade and Dana Carvey—Gillis admitted he was intimidated about going to the gym in New York City, putting a spotlight on women he’s seen working out there.

“I haven’t been to the gym in so long,” he said during the show’s October episode. “I didn’t know women just dressed like wh--es now. Look, I’m sorry. There’s no other way to describe—have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts?”

He added, “Those neon—they’re like artificial bait colored. And the wrinkles go like around the cheeks and all combined at the butthole. And don't look. You're not allowed to look. For real, don't look because they are filming.”

During his latest appearance, Gillis—who was let go from SNL in 2019 just days after his casting was announced due to past comments—also addressed how he handled the backlash he faced this time around.

“The first time I got fired, I kept social media and in my head I was like, ‘That guy talked s--t,'" he explained. "This time, I just deleted everything immediately. So, I don’t really know."

For a closer look at SNL's many hosts, keep reading...

The Kardashians star poked fun at her relationship with ex Kanye West, her connection to O.J. Simpson and her sister Kourtney Kardashian's PDA-heavy romance with now-husband Travis Barker. But she really took flight in an Aladdin-themed sketch that saw her kiss cast member Pete Davidson. The pair would go on to date for nine months.

With 10 hosting gigs under his belt—including the show's first remotely-filmed episode back in April 2020 amid the coronavirus pandemic—you know that when America's Dad is in Studio 8H, you're in for a wonderful time. Don't believe us? We have just three words for you: David. S. Pumpkins.

Hamm left audiences stunned with his considerable comedic chops when he hosted for the first time in 2008. He's has sinced followed up two more times and has had a handful of surprise cameos.

From his unforgettable "Jon Hamm's John Ham" sketch—you know, lunch meat you eat on the toilet—to his live-action Ace in an adaptation of the iconic Ambiguously Gay Duo animated sketch, he's ingratiated himself with cast in a way few other hosts ever have.

There is arguably no one on this planet more committed to their craft than the Bridesmaids legend. Case in point? The "Taste Test" sketch in her first at bat as host, back in 2011, when she covered herself in Hidden Valley ranch dressing for a gag.

In less than a decade, she's already joined the infamous Five-Timers Club, and even began making semi-regular appearances a particularly enraged Sean Spicer during his brief tenure in the Trump administration.

Nearly every celeb on this list could've become a full-time cast member on SNL, easily. And for a time there, it seemed like JT actually might. From "Omletteville," "D--k in a Box," and "Barry Gibb Talk Show" to "Mother Lover," each of Timberlake's five appearances as host made moments that permeated pop culture. And his appearance as one of Beyonce's "Single Ladies" back-up dancers alongside Bobby Moynihan and Andy Samberg? Amazing.

There are few people who have hosted SNL more than the legendary comedian—in fact, there's only one—and in his 16 stints in Studio 8H between 1976 and 2009, he created memorable characters (the "wild and crazy" Festrunk Brothers, King Tut) and delivered what would become one of the show's most heartfelt moments, honoring Gilda Radner's passing from cancer with a look back at a blissful dance the two shared through the studio.

Not only is ScarJo part of the SNL family thanks to her romance with Colin Jost, but the six-time host has created some indelible moments over the years since her debut in 2006.

She's been on hand for whenever the show needed someone to step into Ivanka Trump's shoes, appeared in the grotesque Shud the Mermaid sketch opposite Kate McKinnon and played Lexi (daughter to Fred Armisen's Mark) as the duo hawk chandeliers, ceramic busts, marble columns and porcelain fountains in the fan-favorite sketch.

Unlike everyone else on this list (save for Kim Kardashian), the late TV icon only hosted SNL once. And, at 88 years old, she became the show's oldest host in its history. The appearance was made even more special because it was literally fan-demanded through a successful Facebook campaign after White's role  in The Proposal. She's also on this list because, well, she was freaking hilarious. Our favorite sketch from the episode is this absurd one where Tina Fey's census taker tries, in vain, to get a straight answer out of White.

A member of the Five Timer's Club, Johnson earned his spot on this list the minute he agreed to do The Rock Obama. Enough said.

With 17 official hosting gigs on his resume and countless appearances as former President Donald Trump, Baldwin may be the only star not officially on the payroll who is more closely associated with SNL. From classics like Canteen Boy and Schweddy Balls to impressions of Tony Bennett and, yes, Trump, Baldwin has given fans so much during his many, many visits to Studio 8H.

This Vampire Survivors spin-off has a lot of love for the famous grimdark sci-fi universe, but without the intimidatingly dense lore and complex systems.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've had no shortage of great Warhammer 40K games lately, but most aren't exactly aimed at the casual crowd. Warhammer Survivors changes that, finally providing curious gamers with an easy entry point into the grim darkness of the 41st millennium.

Developed by Auroch Digital (in collaboration with Vampire Survivors' Poncle), this new spin on the survivors-like roguelite subgenre mixes the sci-fi 40,000 setting with the pure fantasy Age of Sigmar universe. This means heroes and enemies from all over the Warhammer mythos meet together in a bite-sized game that anyone can figure out and enjoy in less than five minutes.

When you look at the alternatives, that's a remarkable achievement for a franchise that's notoriously hard (and often expensive) to get into.

Warhammer Survivors isn't bogged down by dense lore, involved mechanics, or massive campaign playthroughs. It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos.

All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula.

If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. You battle an endless onslaught of enemies that slowly march towards you, with your character passively attacking automatically. You only need to move them around sprawling arenas and select level-up upgrades and items after collecting enough gems (skulls in this case).

The moment-to-moment gameplay is as simple as it can get outside of walking sims and interactive "experiences," but there's a deceiving depth to item synergies and how to correctly "build" characters to endure all the carnage.

Unlike Poncle's original game, Warhammer Survivors struggles a bit to get going. The early hours are sluggish until you unlock certain meta upgrades, but its still got that Vampire Survivors magic at its core.

As far as "podcast/gym games" go, this is a perfect fit. There's just enough going on to keep one's brain engaged, but minimal inputs and a tight overarching design lead to a rhythm that's easy to get into without using much brainpower. It's oddly satisfying to weave through enemies and level up your firepower, watching a single Astra Militarum grunt grow into a full Lasgun-spamming, chainsword-wielding wrecking ball.

Achievement and unlock hunters will find enough to bite into here, too. It's unclear if the devs will continue to add more Warhammer 40K and Age of Sigmar deep cuts to this game via DLCs and free updates, but those universes have daunting depths to explore. This really could become a gateway game for future 40K fans: by the time they realize they're hooked, they'll already have 2000 pts of space marines painted and ready to play.

As massive sci-fi and fantasy properties try to aggressively expand and absorb more and more fans, it's easy to pander to already-converted diehards too much. And sure, we can't wait for strategy heavyweights like Dawn of War 4 and Total War: WH40K either, but they're hardly good recommendations for folks who don't even know what a Space Marine is or why the robotic Necrons are so grumpy.

Warhammer Survivors won't answer those questions beyond the surface-level iconography, but it's fun enough to push those curious to dig deeper and embrace the same material in more mature video game genres... and maybe even pick up a few miniatures.

Warhammer Survivors is now available on PC (Steam & GOG), PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 1/2, and mobile (iOS & Android). It's also playable on Game Pass.

#799. Clinical Norway dent Wales’ Nations League top-tier hopes with victory in Oslo

Home side avenge October defeat in Cardiff

Wales bottom of Group A4 with one game left

Wales suffered a 3-1 defeat to Norway in Oslo to dent their hopes of staying in the top tier of the Nations League.

Antonio Nusa and Andreas Schjelderup struck in the space of nine second-half minutes as Norway turned the screw.

Substitute David Brooks halved the deficit 11 minutes from time as Wales finished strongly.

However, Connor Roberts brought down Schjelderup and Erling Haaland converted from the penalty spot, extending his Nations League goals record to 23, as Norway avenged their October defeat in Cardiff.

It means Wales will definitely finish bottom of Group A4, irrespective of Tuesday’s result at home to Portugal.

Although they could finish on six points with Denmark and Norway, they have a worse head-to-head record against both nations – and could now face a playoff in March to avoid relegation to Group B.

#798. What Wales need to stay in Nations League top tier

Having been unbeaten in Craig Bellamy's first nine games, Wales have only won four of their past 16 matches

It can be easy to get tangled up in the complexities of Nations League permutations and, although Wales still have a few uncertainties to iron out, the picture is becoming clearer for Craig Bellamy's side.

Following their 3-1 defeat in Norway on Saturday, Wales will finish bottom of Group A4 even if they win their final game against reigning champions Portugal on Tuesday.

But that does not mean they will definitely be relegated from the top tier.

Instead, they are almost certain to play one of the teams from League B in a relegation play-off in March.

However, one thing is for sure: As a result of the Norway loss, Wales will not be among the top seeds for Euro 2028 qualifying.

"We wanted to be in pot one. That was the drive," said head coach Bellamy after the defeat in Oslo.

"Some people might say, 'what makes you think you should be in pot one?' But I do.

"Maybe I'm naÃ¯ve. I see in big parts of that game we can be in pot one. Let's take the good bits from the game, definitely improve on certain moments of the game and just keep pushing."

A point against Portugal would make sure of it, but even if they lose, Wales will most likely end up in a relegation play-off.

Only the two worst-performing sides will be automatically relegated to League B.

With one game left, the other bottom teams in League A - Turkey, the Czech Republic and Serbia - all have no points, whereas Wales have three.

For them to finish among the worst two, they would need to lose to Portugal, and two of the other teams would need to win their final fixture with a significant swing in goal difference.

Wales have a goal difference of -5. Considering Turkey (-10) visit France, Czech Republic (-10) are in Croatia and Serbia (-7) travel to Greece, it would require an unlikely turn of events for Bellamy's men to be automatically relegated.

Wales have conceded eight goals during this Nations League campaign

The relegation play-offs will be held across two legs at the end of March, with the first leg between March 25-27, and the second between March 28-30.

As a League A side, Wales will be seeded and therefore play at home in the second leg.

The draw for the play-offs takes place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland, on Friday, 20 November.

The sides that finish in the top two of League A's four groups will also discover the quarter-final draw on the same day.

Wales played their part in League A - Bellamy

With one game left to play, it's not yet clear.

Slovenia, Northern Ireland, Kosovo and Bosnia-Herzegovina are currently all in second place in their groups.

However, Scotland, Ukraine, Austria, the Republic of Ireland and Poland could also be potential opponents.

Wales have scored three goals in five games during this Nations League campaign

All teams finishing third or higher in League A will be named as top seeds for Euro 2028 qualifying.

By missing out, Wales could now be drawn alongside one of Europe's heavyweights in their group.

Spain, France, Italy, Netherlands and Portugal are among the sides already guaranteed pot one seeding for the draw on 6 December in Belfast.

England will also be a top seed, although Thomas Tuchel's men will be kept apart from Wales and the other Euro 2028 co-hosts in qualifying regardless.

When it comes to reaching the Euros, the 12 group winners and eight best-ranked runners-up qualify directly.

For any of the co-hosts who don't make it via that route, there are two automatic spots available. Those will be awarded to the best-ranked between the four nations who haven't qualified directly.

If Wales still haven't made it, there is still the back-up option of the play-offs.

And given play-off places are based on Nations League rankings, Wales are highly likely to already have that safety net.

#797. Aaron Rodgers Shares New Photo With Brother Jordan Rodgers After Feud

Aaron Rodgers shared a new photo of himself posing with his younger brother Jordan Rodgers, proving the two are officially on good terms following their yearslong family feud.

Aaron Rodgers and Jordan Rodgers have officially reached a neutral zone.

Months after the Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback revealed he and his family had ended their yearslong estrangement, the NFL star, 42, shared picture-perfect proof of a reunion with his younger brother.

“Great to see little bro @jrodgers11 in his element tonight @acrisurestadium,” Aaron captioned a Nov. 13 Instagram post of the pair. “Really proud of how hard he’s worked to get to where he is now.”

But Aaron and Jordan, 38, weren’t only ones feeling the love as fans were equally as happy to see the two tackle their differences.

“Any girl who’s watched the Bachelorette knows how big of a deal this is,” one person commented, while another added, “Got tears in my eyes over a reunion of two people who don’t know I exist.”

Tensions between the two brothers took center stage after Jordan revealed he didn’t have “much” of a relationship with the athlete while competing on The Bachelorette in 2016.

But earlier this year, Aaron shared that he had decided to huddle up with his family, including older brother Luke Rodgers, once again after his parents Ed Rodgers and Darla Rodgers moved to Nashville.

“There was some stuff there,” Aaron detailed during a Sept. 10 appearance on the Not Just Football podcast, “and I could tell I was coming to a time where I needed to make it right.”

As he explained, “I went to Nashville and met up with my older brother, and a couple weeks after that, met up with my little brother. It was cool. There were tough conversations for sure, but I’m just in a much better headspace.”

Aaron also credited his wife Brittani—whom he announced he had privately married in 2025—with getting him to the end zone.

“She was a big part of that,” he said. “Not that she was pushing anything, she wasn’t. It was more of when you’re loved by someone in such an unconditional way, it changes your perspective on all your relationships surrounding that. It becomes your anchor point.”

As for Jordan, the ESPN commentator also proved there was no longer a line of defense when it came to his brother, quipping about Aaron during an on-air segment in September.

“Rodgers was actually very accurate down the field," the TV personality said during ESPN's First Take on Sept. 23. "The throws that were not completed because of either a non-call or a drop down the field were on the money."

Noting that his commentary on Aaron’s performance might be just a bit biased, Jordan added, "Not trying to be a homer.”

For a closer look into what Aaron has said about his family before reconciling, keep reading...

After growing up "in a really conservative, small-town environment" in Chico, Calif., Aaron Rodgers said in the Netflix docuseries Aaron Rodgers: Enigma, transferring from Butte College to University of California, Berkeley, was admittedly an eye-opening experience for him. "So that was fun, to have my ideologies tested."

But, as he recalled, he was already traveling a path that was taking him further and further away from how he was raised by dad Ed Rodgers and mom Darla Rodgers.

The "white, dogmatic church" he grew up in "didn’t really serve me," Aaron said. "It was very rigid in structure. I'm not a rigid person. Shame, guilt, judgment—it was like, 'We have the truth, our way or the highway, our way is heaven, your way is hell.' Even talking to my parents, it was very black and white. Somebody has to be wrong, somebody has to be right. I just slowly uncoupled from that in high school."

So being in a city like Berkeley "that challenged my beliefs" (and where he was sleeping in on Sunday after games instead of going to church), he continued, "definitely helped me to begin to question more things."

Desperately Seeking Spiritual Enlightenment

After capping off the Green Bay Packers' 2011-12 NFL season with a Super Bowl victory—which, until then, Aaron thought was the holy grail he was seeking—he started to wonder what else was out there.

"I really just desperately wanted to be more than  a football player," he said in the series, "and so I started my spiritual journey."

Aaron got into the teachings of progressive spiritual leader Rob Bell, author of What Is the Bible? (which the athlete is seen reading in the series), and started reading more philosophy and self-help books.

Appreciating what he found to be Rob's inclusive, nonjudgmental approach to faith, "He was a big help for me to totally unravel the religion of my youth," Aaron said in Enigma.

Through his readings, "I found a courage to speak my feelings better," he continued. "So I started to stand up to institutions of my youth, and that was everything from organized religion, my parents, dogma, ideology. That definitely changed the dynamics of my family, because I was just questioning all of it."

Winning a Super Bowl vaulted Aaron to another tier of fame, the athlete recalling how during the summer of 2011 he was "paparazzi'd" for the first time during a trip to Hawaii.

"I was like, 'F--k, life's different now," he said. And after he was on TV more, he added, "my whole ability to move around with relative anonymity changed."

He added, "I didn't do myself any favors with some of the girls I dated after that, that were in the public eye. I definitely hated it at first. Like really despised it. I enjoyed my private life. I enjoyed being able to go places. But from Super Bowl MVP, [league] MVP, State Farm commercials, that got a little more difficult."

While the doc flashed to pictures of him with three famous exes, that was the entirety of what Aaron said about his high-profile relationships with Olivia Munn, Danica Patrick and Shailene Woodley (who, incidentally, he was engaged to and didn't just date).

Olivia, who dated Aaron from 2014 until 2017, denied rumors that she played a role in her ex's estrangement from his family, saying on Andy Cohen Live in 2018, "He hadn't spoken to the parents and one brother for, like, eight months before we started dating."

Aaron reiterated to biographer Ian O'Connor, author of 2024's Out of the Darkness: The Mystery of Aaron Rodgers, that his issues with his family were "deep rooted" and Olivia "has nothing to do with all the years" they haven't spoken.

"There was a lot of times, when I became real famous," Aaron said in Enigma, "where I heard from a lot of people, including family members, who where it was like, ‘Your life is too big, we need you to be smaller. Be smaller, don't talk about your life.'"

Feeling woefully misunderstood, he continued, "It always hurt me because I just feel like you don’t see me. This is not something I ever desired or wanted, other than playing on Sundays. It can definitely change the people around your circle, because it can be intoxicating, the fame and notoriety. So, definitely relationships changed after that. Friendships, family."

Aaron said that, pre-estrangement, he wasn't "super-duper close" with everybody in his family anyway.

"I was close with my little brother," he recalled, referring to younger sibling Jordan Rodgers. "But in actuality it goes back to stuff from high school that kind of made me feel distant. Stuff in college, stuff post-college. And I was quiet about it. 'Cause I thought the best way to do it was, just don’t talk about it publicly. And what do they do?"

In 2016, Jordan appeared on The Bachelorette—and, incidentally, he's been married to rose-bearer JoJo Fletcher since 2022.

When he brought JoJo home to meet his folks and eldest brother Luke Rodgers, there were two empty chairs at the dinner table—purportedly for Aaron and then-girlfriend Olivia—and all of a sudden millions of people found out the Packers QB was estranged from the rest of the family.

"We miss our brother," Luke said on The Bachelorette. "We just are trusting that God brings things full circle. And just wish that everything would just get back to us being a family."

"They go on a bulls--t show and leave two empty chairs," he said in Enigma. "They all agreed this was like a good thing to do, to leave two empty chairs at a stupid dating show that my brother just went on to get famous—his words, not mine—that he ended up winning."

Aaron reiterated in the series that he was never even invited to the dinner, which was held during the NFL season.

A dinner "I was never asked to go to," he said, "not that I would have gone."

E! News reached out to Jordan, Ed and Darla for comment on what Aaron had to say in Enigma but has not yet heard back.

Jordan told E! in 2016 after his hometown episode aired that he "made a commitment to go on there and be honest with JoJo and make sure that she knew everything" about where he was coming from.

Aaron has embraced taking ayahuasca—"It's the hardest medicine possible, that I've tried"—as an essential part of his journey, also touting its healing power for "mind, body, spirit."

"I was searching, for sure," he said in Enigma. "My life was through one lens, of organized religion. Where are people in life finding deep peace and centeredness and presence outside of what I knew?"

Speaking of the divide between him and his family, Aaron said he "found a lot of resistance" once he started researching other religions and plant medicine, "doing things that, compared to what I grew up in, would be considered an alternative lifestyle."

As for his family, he continued, "You know, they’re living as best they can. That is, still engulfed in organized religion, which works for them. That's great. So as much as they might not like what they see, love and respect and gratitude for how I was raised, because it wouldn’t have turned me into who I am today."

"People ask me, 'Is there hope for a reconciliation?'" Aaron said. "I say, 'Yeah, of course. Of course.'"

He added, "I don’t want them to fail, to struggle, to have any strife or issues. I don't wish any ill will on them at all. It's more like this: We're just different steps on the timeline of our own journeys."

#796. Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson

Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival feels like yet another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago

Magnusson: And your time starts ... now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago.

The problem with football is that it never sits still. What was true once isn’t necessarily true now. What is true now won’t necessarily be true in a season or two’s time. Almost nothing is absolute. What works once might not work in a different context. The key to good recruitment is identifying to what extent somebody’s past success was contingent on their environment, and how they may behave in a different circumstances. And that is very difficult, which is why only four managers have won the English league title with more than one club.

The possibility of José Mourinho becoming manager of United was first raised as Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. Mourinho has recently claimed he turned the job down; other versions of events have him raging in a Madrid hotel as he learned that David Moyes had been hired, seemingly because Sir Bobby Charlton, then a senior board member, was worried about his impact on the image of the club.

It’s impossible, of course, to say whether Mourinho would have been a success had he taken the job then. But he had the ego to ensure he would not have lived in Ferguson’s shadow and, although he had been bruised by the Real Madrid experience, English football still recognised his aura. He was still adept enough to win a third league title at Chelsea.

By the time Mourinho finally took the United job in 2016, though, events in his final few months at Stamford Bridge had undermined him. He seemed weary and fractious, the tactical doubts raised in his final year at Madrid had proliferated and there was a growing sense his methods did not quite work with elite modern players.

There was a lot of talk about him as a guaranteed winner, but there’s no such thing in football. Very few managers last more than a decade at the very top. Only the most driven personalities, the most fecund minds, can endure the process of constant evolution necessary to stay ahead of the pack for more than a few years.

It’s easy to see why a board would have looked at his list of honours and been impressed, but United were appointing a manager on the way down. Was that obvious at the time? Perhaps not, but there were warning signs, and it’s the job of those doing the job of recruitment to identify them.

With every appointment there are mitigations. Given the immense power Ferguson had, it would have been hard not to appoint Moyes when he had backed him. Yet if there was ever a time when he might have been the right man for United, it was surely six or seven years earlier; modern managers tend to peak in their mid-late 40s.

Louis van Gaal was 62 when he took the reins at United, enjoying a second coming after winning the Dutch title with AZ Alkmaar and an impressive 2014 World Cup campaign with the Netherlands. Perhaps the comparison isn’t fair in that he arrived as an elder statesman; nobody, other than perhaps Van Gaal, thought he would be a long-term appointment. But the idea he would bring calm after a period of turbulence was to ignore everything he had previously done. Van Gaal is many things but he is not a calming presence.

But again, the timing felt wrong. It could never have worked given he was preparing a side for the World Cup, but had he come in to replace Ferguson in 2013, as a hugely respected figure with a robust self-belief that was never going to care about breaking Fergusonian taboos, he might have been the man to see United through the awkward transition.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim were supposed to be the coming men, managers identified on the way up. Both seemed to make sense. Ten Hag’s Ajax had played astonishing football, had beaten Juventus and Real Madrid thrillingly in the Champions League, had come within Lucas Moura’s implausible hat-trick of a Champions League final. Amorim had ended Sporting’s 19-year title drought.

But it turned out they weren’t right. Ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the job; Amorim’s insistence on playing 3-4-2-1 with a squad ill-equipped to play that way was one of the reasons Dan Ashworth expressed reservations, leading to his departure as sporting director.

It is possible, of course, maybe by this point even likely, that there is no right answer, that the mess United are in is insoluble, Old Trafford a meat grinder that will keep chewing up managerial reputations in perpetuity. But United’s board’s attempts to identify the rising star have been no more successful than their habit of appointing fading legends.

Which brings us to Mauricio Pochettino. He has done remarkable things: he may not yet have won trophies in England but he effected such an extraordinary transformation at Tottenham that it seemed not unreasonable they should be part of the Super League project. He found things difficult at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, but most people do. A last-16 exit at a home World Cup with the USA was about par. The question, now he is 54, is whether the sense of drift about his career is an unfortunate and temporary state, or evidence that he is not quite what he was.

Perhaps the United job will revitalise him and he will revitalise them. But this feels like another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago; that United, once again, are answering the previous question.

#795. Top Chef Alum Leah Cohen’s Husband Ben Byruch Dead at 44

Ben Byruch, a restaurateur and husband to Top Chef alum Leah Cohen, has died at the age of 44: "We will miss him more than words can say."

Leah Cohen and her family are facing a devastating loss.

Ben Byruch—a restaurateur and husband to the Top Chef alum—has died at the age of 44, their company Pig and Khao, which they co-founded, shared Nov. 12.

“We are heartbroken to share the passing of Ben Byruch—husband to our chef and owner Leah Cohen, devoted father, son, brother, and friend to so many,” they wrote in a statement shared to Instagram. “Ben was the co-founder of Pig & Khao and its creative heart. His vision shaped who we are, and his warmth, passion and sense of humor touched everyone lucky enough to know him.”

Cohen—who ultimately placed sixth on the fifth season of Top Chef in 2008—tied the knot with Byruch in July 2016. Three years later, the couple welcomed their oldest son Carter, followed by their youngest son Baker in 2022.

The Great American Recipe judge previously opened up about working alongside her husband to build their businesses within the culinary world.

"Ben was actually hired as my line cook when we first opened and was quickly promoted to sous chef based on his skills," she told Downtown Magazine in 2016. "He was my sous chef for about a year until he made the switch to front of house. It’s much better for our relationship that we aren’t directly working together in the kitchen."

Cohen also shared what made their relationship work both on a professional and personal level.

“It can definitely be hard working with your significant other, but we do a good job of keeping business and personal lives separate,” she continued. “We try not to bring home any work drama, and if we do, we just let it out and then move on.”

Byruch's passing also comes nearly two weeks after she shared insight into a recent trip the couple enjoyed with their loved ones.

"Second time in Hawaii and I’m even more in love," she captioned a Nov. 3 Instagram post featuring photos of the pair with their family. "Huge thank you to @hifoodwinefest for having me back. Getting to cook Filipino food in a place with such deep Filipino roots meant a lot to me, and so many people came up to tell me the food reminded them of home. This is my favorite festival to cook at, and the care you put into the festival, the chefs and the community really shows.""Never in my wildest dreams did I think following my passion for cooking would lead to so many opportunities," she concluded. "I’m grateful I get to do what I love, travel the world, and make these memories with my family."

#794. Declan Rice accepts he had an ‘average World Cup’ as England gear up for Spain showdown

Midfielder needed a break ‘to come back stronger’

James Trafford selected to start in goal for England

Declan Rice has admitted he had an “average” World Cup at the end of a gruelling season and needed time out during the international window in September and October in order to return stronger.

The Arsenal midfielder believes the break has served its purpose, having produced starring performances against Bayern Munich and Liverpool in recent weeks. He is now ready to hit his best level for England in Sunday’s Nations League showdown against Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium.

Rice managed nerve pain in a hamstring that affected his lower back throughout the second half of last season and his fitness was a talking point during the World Cup. The 27-year-old had good games, most notably against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 when he filled in towards the end as an emergency right-back.

Rice played well and scored in the third-place playoff against France. But he was typically honest when asked to reflect on his tournament as he prepared for the Spain game. England will leapfrog the world champions and finish top of their Nations League group if – and only if – they win in Madrid. It would theoretically bring an easier draw for the two-leg quarter-finals in March.

“By my standards it was an average World Cup,” Rice said. “France was probably my best game, Congo I played really well; some of the other games I didn’t play too well but you look back … I played 69 games [in the season].

“A title win with Arsenal, a Champions League final loss and into a World Cup. It’s annoying because at the World Cup you want to be at your best, you want to be totally fresh, you want to be ready. It’s annoying that I couldn’t perform how I did at Arsenal towards the back end of the season.

“But knowing if I’m not going to be at my best, just constantly give 100% for this team, for the badge and you could see that. I loved [the last-16 win in] Mexico. We had the disappointment of Argentina in the semi-final, the second group game against Ghana. It’s games you look back on and think: ‘Could I have done better?’”

The playoff against France was on 18 July. After a short break, Rice reported back to Arsenal and played 45 minutes of the Community Shield against Manchester City on 16 August. When he played the 90 minutes of the defeat at Brighton on 19 September, he “did not feel right at all”, leading to a conversation with Tuchel who stood him down from England’s first four Nations League ties, the first of which was the 3-2 loss against Spain at Wembley. Rice sent a voice note to the England captain, Harry Kane, to explain his absence.

“I had an honest conversation with the boss here [Tuchel], who was really understanding,” Rice said. “He said: ‘Take some time, get yourself ready.’ It was about using that time to come back fitter and stronger. I feel really good now. It’s still like I’m building up to being 100 per cent but it’s closer to that than what I was a few weeks ago, for sure. And over the last few weeks, my performances have picked up.”

Rice, who won his 81st cap in the win over Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, had only previously withdrawn from three England camps. “I know the importance of playing for England, I know the importance of showing up, being available,” he said. “It’s one of the biggest things to me. Last camp, if I didn’t speak to the manager about it, I wouldn’t have done it. But he gave me his word. So I was in a better place mentally knowing that he authorised it.”

Rice has played at least 50 club matches in each of the past five seasons. “It’s something my body has got used to,” he said. “Probably last year, I felt it more than anything in terms of the amount of games, the toll it does take and realising as you get older, you have to take the recovery side of it a lot more seriously. When you were 21, 22, 23 … you could get up and have a round of golf the next day [after a match]. Now, even though I’m young at 27, you get up after a game and you can hardly feel your legs.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Meanwhile, Tuchel has decided to start James Trafford in goal against Spain – an eye-catching decision that will only harden the impression that Jordan Pickford is no longer his first-choice goalkeeper. Tuchel gave them two matches apiece in the September/ October window and said that he was minded to split the minutes once again this time.

When he started Pickford against Croatia, it felt as though he had shelved the plan, given his insistence that the Everton player remained his No1 and Spain is plainly the bigger game. But Tuchel announced at his pre-match conference that Trafford would be given the opportunity.

“Traff will play,” Tuchel said. “We want to see how far Traff is. So he gets a highly competitive match. We had some changes in the back four in the last match [against Croatia], so we went for more stability and more experience with Pickers. And Traff gets the match tomorrow.

“Hopefully he’s not too over-excited or overly nervous because there’s no need to be. We trust him. But it is different to play for England than to play for your club. And to have the opportunity to play matches where it really matters is the best way to show up and to show that you’re ready. We know what Jordan can do for us. Jordan is, at the moment, our No1. I have a very clear picture in high-pressure moments.”

Tuchel also revealed that Ezri Konsa was back in contention after missing the Croatia game with a minor knee problem. He made it sound as though the Arsenal defender would start. “He showed up yesterday for individual work and he showed up today for training,” Tuchel said. “Ezri is back and ready to play.”

#793. Six goals to go - will McGinn catch Dalglish & Law?

As Scotland legend Kenny Dalglish watched one of his records equalled in Scotland's 2-1 win over North Macedonia, another of his feats loomed into view.

The night was supposed to be about Andy Robertson joining Dalglish as Scotland's most-capped man, the Tottenham left-back making his 102nd appearance for his country.

But instead, for the first time, the 75-year-old might be nervous that his crown as one of Scotland men's all-time top goalscorers is wobbling.

That is because, in Scotland's rather humdrum Nations League victory, John McGinn - in his 94th Scotland appearance - took two big strides towards the record.

The Aston Villa midfielder now has 24 goals for his country - six shy of Dalglish's long-standing record of 30, shared with Denis Law.

"It's something that's been in the back of my head," McGinn admitted in the post-match debrief. "If I start climbing that table, it means we've been successful as a team."

Now 32 years old, time is running out for him. But as he pulls level with Hughie Gallacher, one of the Wembley Wizards of folklore, his ambition is clear.

McGinn double gives drab Scotland win over North Macedonia

There was a time when talk of this record being toppled seemed laughable. Scotland has produced strikers in recent decades, but none close to Dalglish or Law.

The fact a midfielder might take the title makes McGinn's feat all the more astonishing.

His prowess in front of goal is no secret to the Tartan Army. There was the spell at the end of 2019 where he scored six in three games, his overhead kick against Austria, his late winner against Croatia in 2024.

But of late, his lack of goals and even his performances have had some fans questioning where he fits into the Scotland team.

"It has been a bit of a dry patch for me over the last year on the goal front," McGinn admitted, and he's not wrong.

He failed to find the back of the net for Scotland in 2025, the first time he'd done that since 2020.

But, just as his form at Villa has sky-rocketed, he came up big for his new international head coach Sebastien Pocognoli.

"Isn't it great to have a John McGinn in your team?" former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on Sportsound. "He's somebody you'd want to have in your team to be taking a penalty for you.

"I'd be surprised if John McGinn doesn't get the goal record now. It might take him another year or two, but he is definitely capable of getting that record."

Becoming Scotland's main penalty taker will help, a fact McGinn alluded to coyly post-match.

In his career, he had only taken one spot-kick before this season - scoring for Scotland in the 3-3 draw against Norway back in 2023.

In this campaign he has scored three and missed one, smacking the bar against Fulham on Halloween.

In classic McGinn fashion, he bounced back to slot home against Manchester United the following week, before being caught on ref-cam admitting to the official that he was nervous to take it after his hitting the woodwork.

That jovial, lovable personality has not just won him fans off the pitch. It is clear that his team-mates at both Villa and the national team adore him.

"He's not going to stop until he [gets the record]," said striker Che Adams, who helped set up McGinn's first against North Macedonia.

"Everyone's pleased for him, he's the best person I've met in football. For him to get the recognition he deserves is amazing."

McGinn's iconic status in Scottish football is secure and will not be tarnished if he fails to climb the mountain.

Whether it is being speared by Steven Thompson in training, calling Scotland performances 'jobby', or admitting he would "probably be at Yeovil" were it not for his backside, the midfielder has already won the heart of a nation.
